sermon:
## Order in the House, Silence to the Liars: The Church That Can Defend Itself (Titus 1)
*Why Paul left a man on Crete instead of a program*

**Text:** Titus 1 · **Supporting:** 1 Timothy 3:1-7 · Acts 20:29-30 · 2 Timothy 4:3-4 · Ezekiel 34:2-4 · Matthew 7:15-16 · Galatians 1:6-9

Crete had a reputation, and Paul quotes it to their faces. A church had been planted on an island whose own poet said its people were liars, and into that church came men who could talk. Fluent, religious, persuasive men who were emptying households of everything solid and filling them with talk. Paul's answer was not a conference. It was not a strategy. It was a person left behind and a standard raised high. We have inherited the opposite instinct. We build platforms and hope character follows. Paul built character and let the platform take care of itself. The difference is not cosmetic. It is the difference between a church that can defend itself and a church that will believe whatever its most gifted voice says next.

### I. The Purpose Behind the Person: Order and Elders (Titus 1:1-9)

Paul does not open Titus with warmth. He opens with weight. Three verses of dense theology, chosen ones, the knowledge of the truth, godliness, the hope of eternal life promised before the ages began, land on a single practical instruction: *"This is why I left you in Crete, so that you might put what remained into order, and appoint elders in every town as I directed you."* (Titus 1:5) The Greek behind *put in order* is *epidiorthoō*, the word for setting a dislocated bone. Something was out of joint. Something needed to be reset, and resetting a bone is not gentle work. It is the kind of care that hurts on the way to healing.

Notice what the remedy is. Not more preaching from Titus. Elders. Plural, appointed, in every town. The health of a church, in Paul's mind, is not secured by one gifted man passing through. It is secured by proven men staying put. Titus was an evangelist, a founder, a mobile apostolic worker, and Paul's instruction to him is essentially to work himself out of a job by raising up local men who would still be there long after Titus sailed away. The measure of the traveling leader is what he leaves standing when he leaves.

And the list that follows in verses 6 through 9 is almost entirely a list of character, not competence. Above reproach. The husband of one wife. Children who are not open to the charge of debauchery. Not arrogant, not quick-tempered, not a drunkard, not violent, not greedy for gain. Hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, disciplined. Read the list slowly and you will notice how ordinary it is. There is nothing in it about charisma, nothing about crowd size, nothing about the man's reach. It is a description of how a man treats his wife, his children, his money, his temper, and his cup.

- **A. The one thing that is not character is competence, and it comes last.** Verse 9: *"He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught, so that he may be able to give instruction in sound doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it."* The single skill required is fidelity to the word, the ability to hold it, teach it, and defend it. And even that is described in terms of grip more than brilliance. He holds firm. He does not innovate the word; he keeps it. Everything else on the list is simply who the man is when no one is watching him teach.
- **B. This is the same standard Paul gives Timothy in Ephesus.** *"The saying is trustworthy: If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task. Therefore an overseer must be above reproach."* (1 Timothy 3:1-2) Two different islands, two different letters, one unbending bar. Paul is not building a resume filter. He is describing a life the congregation can safely follow into the fire. An elder is a man you can imitate without regret, which is why the standard cannot be lowered without lowering the whole church that follows him.

### II. The Reason for the Standard: The Liars Are Already Inside (Titus 1:10-16)

The standard is high because the threat is real, and Paul names it without softening. *"For there are many who are insubordinate, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision party. They must be silenced, since they are upsetting whole families by teaching for shameful gain what they ought not to teach."* (Titus 1:10-11) *Empty talkers*, *mataiologoi*, men whose words are hollow, sound with no substance. And the damage is domestic. Whole families, whole households, overturned. Not the abstract church out there. The dinner table. The deceiver's specialty is not the auditorium. It is the living room, the small group, the private conversation where a family's confidence is quietly dismantled one clever question at a time.

Paul knew this was coming, because he had warned it was coming. To the Ephesian elders at Miletus he had said, weeping, *"I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock; and from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things, to draw away the disciples after them."* (Acts 20:29-30) From among your own selves. The wolf does not always come as an outsider with a snarl. Often he comes as an insider with a Bible verse and a warm handshake and a slightly different gospel. Paul had already told Timothy the appetite for this was in the pews themselves: *"the time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions."* (2 Timothy 4:3) The deceiver never arrives against the will of the flock. He arrives to give them what they were already itching to hear.

- **A. Paul then quotes a pagan and turns it into a diagnosis.** *"One of the Cretans, a prophet of their own, said, 'Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons.' This testimony is true."* (Titus 1:12-13) He is not sneering at an ethnicity. He is refusing to pretend the culture was neutral. The deceivers were fluent in a culture already comfortable with the lie, and Paul will not flatter it. He names it so the church can see what it is up against. A shepherd who will not name the wolf is a hireling, and Ezekiel already indicted the shepherds who fed themselves and not the flock (Ezekiel 34:2-4). Paul is the opposite shepherd. He looks the danger in the face and calls it by name.
- **B. The tell is the gap between profession and life.** *"They profess to know God, but they deny him by their works. They are detestable, disobedient, unfit for any good work."* (Titus 1:16) This is Jesus' own test, *"You will recognize them by their fruits"* (Matthew 7:16), pressed into a single sentence. The empty talker's problem was never his fluency. It was that his life contradicted his mouth, and Crete could not tell the difference until Paul told them the difference. That is exactly why the elder qualifications are what they are. A church that has learned to read character in its leaders has learned the one skill that exposes the deceiver, because the deceiver can counterfeit the words and never the life.

### III. The Church That Cannot Defend Itself: A Word to Us (Living Well in a Post-Christian Culture)

Here is where I have to stop describing Crete and turn around, because we have built exactly the church Paul was trying to prevent. We are magnificent at platforms and terrible at eldership. We can spot a compelling communicator across a screen in six seconds. We cannot tell you whether the man is faithful to his wife, patient with his children, or honest about money, and increasingly we have decided those things are private and therefore beside the point. Paul would call them the point. The competence dazzles us; the character is what protects us, and we have inverted the two. We have made the last item on Paul's list the first item on ours, and we wonder why our most gifted men keep falling and taking whole congregations down with them.

Consider what the fourth-century church did when it faced its own fluent deceivers. When Arius taught, persuasively and popularly, that the Son was a created being, a gospel just slightly off, the church did not run a marketing campaign against him. It called the Council of Nicaea in 325 AD, and it labored over a single word. *Homoousios*, of the same substance. One word, because the empty talkers had made everything hang on precision, and precision is what the deceiver cannot survive. That is Titus 1:9 in action. Hold firm to the trustworthy word, so that you are able to rebuke those who contradict it. The church that could name the lie survived. The church that could not would have dissolved into whatever its most persuasive voice was selling that year. We flatter ourselves that we are past such fights. We are not. We have simply outsourced them to whoever has the largest audience.

- **A. And I will not pretend I stand outside this.** I have been impressed by the wrong things in a leader, my own gifts included. I have measured a man by the room he could hold instead of the home he actually kept, and I have done it from a pulpit that is supposed to know better. I have wanted the church to be exciting more than I have wanted it to be sound, and those are not the same wish. The instinct Paul is correcting is not out there in the deceivers. It is in me, and it is in every congregation that would rather have a show than a shepherd.
- **B. This is why the standard is grace, not law.** The elder who is above reproach is not a man who earned it. He is a man the grace of God has trained, the same grace Paul is about to describe in chapter 2. The trustworthy word Titus must guard is not a rulebook. It is the announcement that Christ gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify a people of his own possession. The false teachers profess God and deny him by their works. The true elder is simply a man in whom the profession and the works have finally started to match, because grace has been at work on him longer than anyone was watching. Order in the house is not the enemy of grace. It is what grace looks like once it has had time to build something.

Character qualifies. Empty talk must stop.

## The Doctrine That Adorns: How Grace Trains the People It Saves (Titus 2)
*The gospel that changes how you set the table*

**Text:** Titus 2 · **Supporting:** Titus 3:4-7 · 1 Peter 2:11-12 · Ephesians 2:8-10 · Romans 6:1-2 · 1 Corinthians 10:31 · Philippians 2:12-13

We have been told for a generation that doctrine divides and love unites, that theology is for the classroom and life is for the street. Paul had never heard of that arrangement. He tells Titus to *"teach what accords with sound doctrine"* (Titus 2:1) and then, having said the word doctrine, immediately talks about old men and young women and slaves and how they carry themselves in the kitchen and the market. In Paul's mind there is no gap between the truth you believe and the way you behave at a funeral. Sound doctrine has a shape, and the shape is a life. The chapter is one long argument that grace is not only a rescue. It is a school. And the graduates of that school are known not by what they can explain but by how they live in a world that is watching.

### I. Sound Doctrine Reaches Every Kind of Person (Titus 2:1-10)

Paul does not give Titus a sermon to preach to the crowd. He gives him a household to instruct, one category at a time. Older men are to be sober-minded, dignified, self-controlled, sound in faith, in love, and in steadfastness. Older women likewise reverent, not slanderers, not slaves to much wine, teaching what is good, and specifically training the younger women to love their husbands and children. Younger men get a single word: self-controlled. Even bondservants, in a Roman world that gave them no dignity at all, are addressed as moral agents whose ordinary honesty preaches. Paul reaches into the lowest, least regarded corner of the household and tells a slave that the way he handles his master's property is theology on display. There is a quiet dignity in that. A world that saw the slave as furniture is told, through Paul, that this man's small daily faithfulness is doing more theological work than the philosophers in the forum. The gospel does not wait for a change of station to make a life matter. It makes the life matter where it stands.

And Paul gives the reason each time, which is the heartbeat of the chapter. The younger women are trained *"that the word of God may not be reviled"* (Titus 2:5). Titus himself is to be a model of good works *"so that an opponent may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say about us"* (Titus 2:8). The bondservants are to be faithful *"so that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior."* (Titus 2:10) Three times, the reason is the watching world. The behavior is not for the believer's comfort. It is for the outsider's eyes.

- **A. That word adorn is the pivot of the whole chapter.** The Greek is *kosmeō*, the root of our word cosmetic, to arrange, to order, to make beautiful. It is what a woman does with jewelry and what God did with the cosmos. Paul says a slave's honesty over a handful of grain makes the doctrine of God beautiful to people watching. Doctrine has an appearance in the world, and that appearance is the ordered lives of ordinary believers. The truth is not made beautiful by our arguments. It is made beautiful by our conduct, and an unbeliever will see the second long before he ever hears the first.
- **B. Peter says the identical thing to scattered exiles.** *"Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable, so that when they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day of visitation."* (1 Peter 2:12) The watching world does not first read your theology. It reads your marriage, your temper, your work, the way you treat a waiter and a rival and a stranger who cannot repay you. Paul is not lowering doctrine to ethics. He is saying doctrine that never becomes a life was never believed. Whatever you can articulate and never obey, you do not actually hold. You are only quoting it.

### II. The Grace That Trains Us to Say No (Titus 2:11-14)

Then comes the engine. Everything in the first ten verses runs on the four verses that follow, and they are among the densest in the New Testament. *"For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age, waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ."* (Titus 2:11-13)

Grace *appeared*, *epephanē*, the language of a sunrise, a dawning, the thing that was hidden now visible. Grace is not a concept Paul argues toward. It is an event that happened, a light that came up over the world at a particular time in a particular manger. And this grace, Paul says, is *training* us. The word is *paideuō*, the word for raising a child, disciplining a son, the whole long formation of a person over years. Grace is not only the verdict that saves. Grace is the teacher that raises. We have been trained by our era to hear grace as permission, grace means I am accepted as I am, and there the sentence stops. Paul does not stop there. Grace teaches. And the first thing it teaches is the word no.

- **A. Renounce ungodliness. Say no.** This is Paul's answer to the oldest objection against grace, the one he faced in Rome: *"Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means."* (Romans 6:1-2) Grace that leaves you exactly as it found you is not the grace of God. The same mercy that pardons the sin sets about, patiently and over years, dismantling it. Grace that never says no to you was never grace. It was only a warm word for being left alone. A father who never disciplines a son he loves is not more loving. He is more absent, and Titus 2 will not let us mistake the absence for kindness.
- **B. And the reason grace gives is the redemption itself.** *"Who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works."* (Titus 2:14) He did not die to accept you and abandon you. He died to buy you and to make you his, a purified people, a possession, zealous. The cross is not only the ground of pardon. It is the ground of the whole new life. This is not works added to grace. This is what grace was always for. Whatever you do with a knife and a bowl of water when you eat, Paul told Corinth, do it all to the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31), because the God who bought the whole of you means to have the whole of you.

### III. The Age That Cannot Say No (Living Well in a Post-Christian Culture)

Turn around with me, because our moment has built an entire understanding of freedom out of the refusal to renounce anything. To say no to a desire, we are told, is to betray yourself; the desire is the truest thing about you, and formation is oppression. The philosopher Charles Taylor, in his 2007 book A Secular Age, described a whole civilization organized around the conviction that each self must express its own inner longings, and that anyone who trains, restrains, or says no to those longings is doing violence to a person. That is the water we swim in. Into that air Paul speaks a scandalous sentence. The grace of God trains us to renounce. Grace teaches the very no our culture has learned to call a wound.

And I feel the pull, so I will not preach this from a safe distance. There is a version of the pastor's job that is all comfort and no formation, all you are accepted and never you are being trained, and I have preferred it, because renounce is a harder word to preach than affirmed, and it costs me the room's affection to say it. I have watered down Titus 2 in my own study before I ever stood to preach it, and I have done it to be liked. When the church stopped believing grace trains us, it did not become more gracious. It became more shapeless, indistinguishable from the culture it was sent to reach, and therefore useless to it.

Consider the early Christians whom the Roman world could not understand, the believers who in the plague of 251 AD stayed in the cities to nurse the dying while the pagans fled, the ones the bishop Dionysius of Alexandria recorded caring for strangers at the cost of their own lives, carrying the sick in their arms and closing the eyes of the dead. That was not grace as permission. That was grace as training, a people who had learned to say no to self-preservation because they were waiting for a better appearing. They adorned the doctrine with their dying, and it was that dying, historians tell us, that made the watching empire ask what kind of God produces such people. We can barely adorn the same doctrine with our patience in traffic.

- **A. The waiting is what makes the saying-no possible.** Paul roots the whole ethic in the return, *waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior.* You can only renounce a present passion if you are anchored to a future glory. Cut the future and the present desire becomes absolute, because it is all there is. This is why an age that has stopped waiting for God cannot say no to itself. It has nothing on the other side of the appetite, so the appetite becomes the whole horizon. Notice too what Paul calls Jesus here, *our great God and Savior.* He is not describing a moral teacher whose example we admire. He is describing the God who will appear in glory, and it is the certainty of that appearing, not the strength of our willpower, that makes renunciation anything more than white-knuckled denial. We do not say no to the world because the world is worthless. We say no because Someone better is coming, and we would rather have him.
- **B. Christ is the whole of it, beginning and end.** He is the grace that appeared at Bethlehem and the glory that will appear at the end. Between those two appearings, he is training a people for his own possession. Not a people who earned him. A people he purchased, and is now, slowly, teaching to walk. Paul's ethics are never bootstraps, *for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure* (Philippians 2:13). They are the long, patient work of a Redeemer finishing what the cross began, in people who could never have started it themselves.

Grace teaches us to say no.

## Saved by Mercy, Ready for Good: The Only Order That Holds (Titus 3)
*Why the rescued life is a useful life, and why the sequence cannot be reversed*

**Text:** Titus 3 · **Supporting:** Ephesians 2:8-10 · Titus 2:14 · John 3:5 · Romans 3:20-24 · Galatians 5:15 · 1 Corinthians 6:9-11

There are two ways to ruin the Christian life, and they are exact opposites. One is to say we are saved by our good works, which crushes the sinner under a weight he cannot carry and hands him a religion that is really just anxiety with a steeple on top. The other is to say that because we are saved by mercy, good works do not matter, which leaves the sinner exactly as ruined but now comfortable about it, sleeping soundly in a house that is still on fire. One error works you to death. The other flatters you to death. Titus 3 refuses both in a single breath. Paul says be ready for every good work, and then, before the paragraph ends, he says you were saved by mercy and not by works of righteousness you had done. Same passage. Same author. No contradiction. The good works are real and required. They are just not the reason God rescued you. Get the order wrong and you lose the gospel. Get it right and you get a life.

### I. The Command: Be Ready for Every Good Work (Titus 3:1-2)

Paul opens the last chapter with the posture of the redeemed in a hostile world. *"Remind them to be submissive to rulers and authorities, to be obedient, to be ready for every good work, to speak evil of no one, to avoid quarreling, to be gentle, and to show perfect courtesy toward all people."* (Titus 3:1-2) Notice the direction of it. Outward. Toward rulers who were pagan, toward neighbors who slandered them, toward all people, a phrase that on Crete meant liars and evil beasts and lazy gluttons, the very people Paul had named in chapter 1. Paul does not tell the church to withdraw from a culture that despised it. He tells the church to be conspicuously good to it.

*Ready for every good work*, the word is *hetoimos*, prepared, standing by, like a servant already dressed and waiting at the door. Not good works someday. Ready now. And the tone is disarming: gentle, no quarreling, perfect courtesy toward everyone. This is a church surrounded by people who despise it, and Paul's instruction is not to fight back but to be useful, gentle, and impossible to accuse. The reflex of the wounded is to snap. The reflex of the redeemed is to serve.

- **A. Gentleness toward all is not weakness. It is doctrine.** The false teachers of chapter 1 were quarrelsome and greedy. The redeemed of chapter 3 are gentle and generous. The contrast is the whole point. You can tell the difference between the empty talker and the real Christian by what happens in an argument, because grace produces a person who has nothing to defend and no one to destroy. The man who has been forgiven everything has been freed from the need to win everything. And this is not the gentleness of a man with no convictions. Paul is the same apostle who told the Galatians to let the false teacher be accursed. The gentleness here is not the absence of truth. It is the presence of a man so secure in mercy he no longer needs to be cruel to be right.
- **B. Paul commands quarrel-avoidance because he knows what quarrels do to a church.** *"If you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another."* (Galatians 5:15) The threat to a small church surrounded by enemies is rarely the enemies. It is the biting inside. Be gentle toward all, including, Paul means, the brother across the aisle who is getting on your nerves, and the sister whose theology on the disputable thing is not quite yours. More churches have died of internal biting than of external persecution.

### II. The Ground: Because This Is What We Were (Titus 3:3-7)

Then Paul does the thing that makes this chapter unforgettable. He tells you why you can afford to be gentle toward liars and beasts, and the reason is a mirror. *"For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray, slaves to various passions and pleasures, passing our days in malice and envy, hated by others and hating one another."* (Titus 3:3) We ourselves. Not them. Us. Before you sneer at Crete, Paul says, remember you were Crete. The malice, the envy, the hating and being hated, that was your address. Paul does not exempt himself, the apostle who had once dragged Christians to prison. He writes we, and he means it.

And then the hinge of the entire letter, one of the great salvation sentences in Scripture. *"But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that being justified by his grace we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life."* (Titus 3:4-7) Everything hangs on that single word *but*. On one side of it, foolish, disobedient, enslaved. On the other side, saved, washed, justified, made an heir. And the only thing that crossed the divide was the mercy of God.

- **A. Read the sequence and never reverse it.** *Not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy.* This is Ephesians 2 in miniature, *"by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast."* (Ephesians 2:8-9) The good works commanded in verse 1 do not appear until after the mercy of verse 5. Works are the fruit of the rescue, never its root. Paul had already spent the opening of Romans establishing that *by works of the law no human being will be justified* (Romans 3:20). Reverse the order and you have built a religion of earning that the cross came to demolish.
- **B. The washing is regeneration, not decoration.** *Palingenesia*, new birth, being made again, the same reality Jesus pressed on Nicodemus: *"Unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God."* (John 3:5) God did not improve the foolish, disobedient, hating creature of verse 3. He washed it, birthed it new, poured out his Spirit richly. That is why the redeemed can be gentle toward the very sins they were drowning in. They know they did not climb out. They were lifted, dripping, by a hand that reached down before they ever reached up. And notice the last word of the sentence, *heirs.* He did not merely acquit the guilty and send them home. He made them family, and wrote them into the will. That is the distance mercy travels: from foolish and enslaved to heir of eternal life, and not one inch of it earned.

### III. The People Who Forgot They Were Rescued (Living Well in a Post-Christian Culture)

Turn the mirror. The great danger for a church that has been saved a long time is that it forgets it was ever drowning, and a people who forget they were rescued become the harshest people alive. They begin to divide, to quarrel over the controversies Paul tells Titus in verse 9 to avoid, the foolish debates and genealogies and quarrels about the law that are unprofitable and worthless. They become experts at spotting the liar across the street and blind to the malice at their own table. I know this church because I have pastored inside it and I have been it. I have felt contempt for a sinner whose exact sin I committed a decade before he did, and I called my contempt discernment, and I did it as a man who preaches Titus 3:3 on Sundays.

This is the sickness the gospel cured at its very beginning, and the record is specific. Paul wrote to a Corinthian church full of people who had been idolaters, adulterers, thieves, drunkards, revilers, and he said, *"And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God."* (1 Corinthians 6:11) Such were some of you. The past tense is the whole secret. The believer who keeps the memory of the mud stays gentle. The believer who forgets it turns cruel. And history bears the warning out: the church has been most vicious in exactly the eras when it was most established, most respectable, most certain it stood on higher ground than the sinner outside the walls. The believer who most needs Titus 3 is not the young convert but the settled saint who has been respectable so long he can no longer remember being a slave to his passions. Verse 3 is the medicine, and we stop taking it precisely when we think we have outgrown it.

- **A. Be ready for good works, but never to be seen doing them.** Paul closes the letter, in verse 14, with a plain word: *"Let our people learn to devote themselves to good works, so as to help cases of urgent need, and not be unfruitful."* Cases of urgent need. Not projects that photograph well. The rescued life spends itself on the ordinary emergencies of ordinary people, quietly, because it is not trying to earn anything. It already has everything. It is simply useful now, the way the healed are useful, not to prove they are well, but because they are.
- **B. Christ is the mercy, and the mercy is the order.** He saved us according to his own mercy, poured out his Spirit through Jesus Christ our Savior, justified us by his grace. Every command in this chapter hangs on that one indicative. First the rescue, then the readiness. Never the readiness to secure the rescue. The moment we invert it we are back in verse 3, hating and being hated, working to earn a mercy that was always meant to be received with empty hands. The gospel is an order that cannot be reversed without ceasing to be the gospel. Salvation first, entirely by his mercy and none of ours. Then, and only then, the good works of people who have nothing left to prove and everything already given.

He saved us. Now be ready.
